title: Eiffel Tower: stairs or lift, second floor or summit?
subtitle: How to choose your way up the tower that Paris once wanted torn down.
excerpt: Three levels, two ways up and a dozen ticket names. What each choice gives you on the Eiffel Tower, how long it takes, and which visit suits which traveller.
longtail_phrases: is the Eiffel Tower summit worth it

Eiffel Tower stairs or lift which is better
how long does an Eiffel Tower visit take
meta_title: Eiffel Tower: stairs or lift, 2nd floor or summit?
meta_description: Stairs or lift, second floor or summit: what each Eiffel Tower ticket really gives you, how long it takes and which one fits your visit.

featured_image.alt: The Eiffel Tower seen from the Champ de Mars on a clear day

content_html:
[place attraction="eiffel-tower" city="paris"]

In February 1887, before a single girder stood on the Champ de Mars, some of the best-known names in French culture signed a letter against it. Guy de Maupassant, Charles Garnier, the architect of the Opera, and Alexandre Dumas the younger called the future tower useless and monstrous, a black factory chimney that would humiliate Notre-Dame and the Louvre. The tower went up anyway, in two years and two months, for the World's Fair of 1889. It was meant to stand for twenty years and then come down.

The tower in 1888, a year before the fair, photographed by Louis-Emile Durandelle. Photo: Louis-Emile Durandelle, via Wikimedia Commons.

It is still there because it turned out to be a very good radio mast. And the question visitors ask today is no longer whether it should exist, but something more practical: which way up, and how far?

Three levels, and what each one is for

The tower has three public levels, and they are not three versions of the same view.

  • The first floor, 57 metres up. The widest platform and the calmest. Parts of the floor are glass, so you can look straight down between your feet at the people queuing below. Most visitors hurry past it on the way up and enjoy it on the way down.
  • The second floor, about 115 metres up. The view most people have in mind when they picture Paris from above. You are high enough to read the whole city, the bend of the Seine, the dome of the Invalides, Sacré-Cœur on its hill, and still low enough to pick out single buildings and streets.
  • The summit, 276 metres up. A different experience: the city flattens into a map and the horizon curves. Up here is the small office Gustave Eiffel kept for himself, where he received guests such as Thomas Edison, shown today with wax figures behind glass.

Stairs or lift?

The stairs run inside one of the pillars, in the open air, from the ground to the second floor: 674 steps. They stop there. Nobody walks to the summit; the last stretch is always a lift that leaves from the second floor.

The stairs are not the hard option they sound like. The climb is broken into short flights with landings, it takes most people 30 to 45 minutes with stops, and it is the only way to see the tower from the inside: 18,000 iron parts held by two and a half million rivets, with the city sliding into view between the girders as you go. The queue for the stairs is also usually the shorter one.

The stairs climb inside the iron lattice, in the open air. Photo: Guilhem Vellut, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The lift is the right choice if you are travelling with small children or anyone who does not manage stairs well, if you are afraid of heights (the staircase is open to the air, behind mesh), or simply if your legs have already had a day of Paris.

These are the ways up that our partner sells for the tower, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="eiffel-tower" match="eiffel" limit="6"]

What the ticket names actually mean

Ticket names for the tower look alike, and the differences matter once you are standing at the gate.

  • "Second floor by stairs" is the climb described above. With the listings that come with a host, you meet a short walk from the tower, hear its story on the way in, and are then left free on the second floor for as long as you like.
  • "Second floor + optional summit" takes you up by lift. Read the word optional carefully: on these listings the summit is an add-on that has to be chosen when you book. If you leave it out, you cannot add it at the top.
  • "Audio tour" listings are a guide in your phone. Some include the entry ticket and some do not, and they say so in their description. An audio tour without a ticket still means buying your entry separately, so check before you pay.

Is the summit worth it?

It depends on what you came for. If you want the photograph of Paris, the second floor gives you the better one: closer, sharper, with the landmarks at a readable size. If you want the feeling of having gone all the way up, and you are curious about Eiffel's office, take the summit. Two things are worth knowing before you decide:

  • The summit lift has its own queue on the second floor, and at busy times that wait is added to everything else. Count on a visit of around two and a half to three hours with the summit, against about an hour and a half without it.
  • The summit closes in strong wind and sometimes in bad weather, at short notice. A second-floor visit is almost never affected.

From the second floor the city is still close enough to read: the Seine, downstream. Photo: Ajayy99, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

When to go

The first slot of the morning has the shortest lines. The hour before sunset has the best light, and it lets you see the city by day, at dusk and lit up in a single visit. After dark the tower sparkles for five minutes at the start of every hour, which you see best from the ground, from the Trocadéro across the river, or from the lawns of the Champ de Mars.

Opening hours change with the season. The current ones, with the address and what else is within walking distance, are on our page for the Eiffel Tower.

Before you go

  • Everyone passes a security check to enter the fenced area under the tower, with or without a ticket. Arrive 20 to 30 minutes before the time on yours.
  • Large bags and suitcases are not allowed and there is no left-luggage office at the tower.
  • It is colder and windier at the top than on the ground, in every season. Bring a layer.
  • The tower is repainted by hand roughly every seven years, and one section or another is often under work. It does not close for that.

The rest of the day

The tower takes a morning or an evening, not a day. The Seine is at its foot, the Musée du quai Branly is five minutes along the river, and the Invalides and the Rodin Museum are a pleasant walk away. To see what else Paris has within reach, or to fit the tower into a longer trip, open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Benh Lieu Song, via Wikimedia Commons.

faqs.q: How many steps are there to the second floor of the Eiffel Tower?
faqs.a: There are 674 steps from the ground to the second floor. The stairs end there: the summit can only be reached by lift from the second floor.

faqs.q: Can you walk all the way to the top of the Eiffel Tower?
faqs.a: No. Visitors can climb the stairs to the second floor. From there to the summit everyone takes the lift.

faqs.q: Is the Eiffel Tower summit worth it?
faqs.a: The second floor has the better view for photographs, because the landmarks are closer. The summit is worth it for the height itself and for Gustave Eiffel's office. It adds about an hour to the visit and can close in strong wind.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Eiffel Tower take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the second floor, and two and a half to three hours if you also go to the summit, including security and the wait for the lifts.

faqs.q: Does an Eiffel Tower audio tour include the entry ticket?
faqs.a: Not always. Some audio tours are sold with a ticket and some without. The description of each one says which, so check before you book.

title: Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel: how to visit without losing half a day in line
subtitle: Seven kilometres of galleries, one chapel at the end, and a queue you can walk past.
excerpt: Where the entrance really is, what a fast track ticket does and does not do, the route to the Sistine Chapel and what to stop for on the way.
longtail_phrases: how to visit the Vatican Museums without waiting in line
how long do the Vatican Museums take
where is the entrance to the Vatican Museums
can you take photos in the Sistine Chapel
meta_title: Vatican Museums & Sistine Chapel: visit without the queue
meta_description: Where the entrance is, what fast track tickets do, the route to the Sistine Chapel and what to see on the way. A practical guide to the Vatican Museums.

featured_image.alt: The entrance to the Vatican Museums in the Vatican walls on Viale Vaticano

content_html:
[place attraction="vatican-museums" city="rome"]

In January 1506 a man digging in his vineyard on the Esquiline Hill broke through into a buried room and found a marble group of a man and his two sons being crushed by serpents. Pope Julius II sent his architect and a young sculptor called Michelangelo to look at it. They recognised the Laocoön, a statue ancient writers had praised as the finest in Rome. The pope bought it within weeks and put it on show in a courtyard of his palace.

The Laocoon, found in 1506, where the collection began. Photo: Fallaner, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

That courtyard is where the Vatican Museums begin. Five centuries later they hold one of the largest art collections on earth, laid out along roughly seven kilometres of galleries, and at the very end of the route stands the room most visitors came for: the Sistine Chapel.

They are also one of the most crowded museums in Europe. A visit goes well or badly depending on a few decisions made before you arrive.

First: the entrance is not in St Peter's Square

This catches people every day. The museums are entered from Viale Vaticano, on the north side of the Vatican walls, about fifteen minutes on foot from St Peter's Square. The nearest metro stops are Ottaviano and Cipro, both on line A.

St Peter's Basilica is a separate visit with its own entrance on the square and its own security line. It is free to enter. A museum ticket does not include it and does not let you skip its line.

What "fast track" and "skip the line" really mean

On a busy morning the line of people without a reservation runs along the walls for hundreds of metres, and waiting two hours is not unusual. A ticket booked in advance for a set time lets you walk past that line to the entrance for reserved visitors.

It does not skip the security check, which everybody passes, so arrive 15 to 20 minutes before your time. With some listings a host meets you at a meeting point near the entrance, walks you through the right door and leaves you to visit on your own; others send the ticket to your phone and you go straight in.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the museums, with today's prices:

[partner q="vatican museums" match="vatican" limit="6"]

A note on reading the listings. A ticket with an audio tour adds a guide that plays in your phone as you walk; bring earphones. And an audio tour sold without a ticket is only the commentary: you still need to book your entry separately, so check the description before you pay.

The route, and what to stop for

The museums are arranged as a one-way walk that ends at the Sistine Chapel. You cannot start with the chapel and you cannot easily go back, so it helps to know what lies along the way.

  • The Pio-Clementino Museum. The ancient sculpture, and the octagonal courtyard where the Laocoön still stands, a few steps from the Apollo Belvedere. Michelangelo studied the muscular Belvedere Torso in the next room so closely that you will see it again, painted, on the chapel ceiling.
  • The Gallery of Maps. A corridor 120 metres long, painted in the early 1580s with forty maps of the regions of Italy under a gilded vault. It is the stretch people photograph most, and it is on everyone's route.
  • The Raphael Rooms. Four rooms painted by Raphael and his workshop for Julius II and his successors, while Michelangelo was working on the ceiling a few doors away. The School of Athens is here: Plato and Aristotle at the centre of a crowd of philosophers, with Raphael himself looking out from the right edge.
  • The Sistine Chapel. Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, standing on a scaffold of his own design, and came back more than twenty years later to paint the Last Judgment on the altar wall. It is still a working chapel: this is where the cardinals meet in conclave to elect a pope.

Look up in the Gallery of Maps: the vault is as crowded as the walls. Photo: Alvesgaspar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The School of Athens, in the Raphael Rooms. Photo: Maksim Sokolov, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Even walking steadily, the route is about two kilometres. Allow three hours for a visit that includes these four stops, and longer if you also want the painting gallery or the Egyptian and Etruscan collections, which lie off the main path.

Rules that are enforced

  • Dress. Shoulders and knees covered, for everyone. Visitors are turned away at the door for this, ticket or not.
  • The Sistine Chapel. No photographs and no filming, and silence is asked for. The guards repeat it all day.
  • Bags. Large backpacks, umbrellas and tripods go to the cloakroom, which is free. You collect them at the entrance, so plan to come back that way.

When to go

The museums are closed on most Sundays. On the last Sunday of the month entry is free, and the line is the longest of the whole month. The quietest times are usually the first slot of the day and mid-afternoon on a weekday, when the morning groups have left. Days and hours change around religious holidays; the current ones are on our page for the Vatican Museums.

After the museums

You leave down a double spiral staircase from 1932, two ramps wound around each other so that people going up never meet people coming down. From the exit it is a short walk to St Peter's Square, and a pleasant twenty minutes along the river to Castel Sant'Angelo. For the rest of the city, see everything there is to do in Rome, or put the Vatican into a longer route with the trip planner for Italy.

The way out: the double spiral staircase of 1932. Photo: Colin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Cover photo: Lalupa, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Where is the entrance to the Vatican Museums?
faqs.a: On Viale Vaticano, on the north side of the Vatican walls, about fifteen minutes on foot from St Peter's Square. The nearest metro stops are Ottaviano and Cipro on line A.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel take?
faqs.a: About three hours for the main route with the sculpture collection, the Gallery of Maps, the Raphael Rooms and the Sistine Chapel. Allow longer for the painting gallery and the other collections.

faqs.q: Does a Vatican Museums ticket include St Peter's Basilica?
faqs.a: No. The basilica is a separate visit with its own entrance on St Peter's Square and its own security line. Entry to the basilica is free.

faqs.q: Can you take photos in the Sistine Chapel?
faqs.a: No. Photography and filming are not allowed in the Sistine Chapel, and visitors are asked to keep silent. Photos without flash are allowed in most other rooms of the museums.

faqs.q: What is the dress code for the Vatican Museums?
faqs.a: Shoulders and knees must be covered, for all visitors. People are refused entry for this even with a valid ticket.

title: The Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Palatine: one ticket, one long walk through ancient Rome
subtitle: What you are looking at, in what order to see it, and when an audio guide in your phone is enough.
excerpt: The arena, the square where Rome was governed and the hill where it began sit side by side. How to see the three in one visit, and what an audio walk adds.
longtail_phrases: how long to visit the Colosseum Roman Forum and Palatine Hill
is a Colosseum audio tour worth it
what order to visit Colosseum Forum Palatine
does a Colosseum ticket include the Roman Forum
meta_title: Colosseum, Roman Forum & Palatine: how to visit all three
meta_description: One visit covers the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill. What to see, in what order, how long it takes and when an audio tour is enough.

featured_image.alt: The Colosseum in Rome in the early evening

content_html:
[place attraction="colosseum" city="rome"]

When the emperor Titus opened the new amphitheatre in the year 80, the games went on for a hundred days. Ancient writers count the animals killed in them in the thousands. The building held around fifty thousand people, who came in through eighty arches at ground level and could, by modern estimates, be seated or sent home again in a matter of minutes.

Its real name is the Flavian Amphitheatre, after the family of emperors who built it. "Colosseum" came later, most likely from a colossal bronze statue of Nero that stood beside it. The statue is gone. The nickname stayed.

What many visitors do not realise until they arrive is that the Colosseum is one third of a single site. Next to it lie the Roman Forum, the square where the republic and then the empire were run, and above the Forum the Palatine Hill, where the emperors lived and where, according to legend, Romulus founded the city. They are seen together, and they make more sense together.

What you are looking at

The Colosseum

An oval 189 metres long and 156 wide, with an outer wall 48 metres high on the side that still stands. The other side came down in an earthquake in 1349, and its stone was carried off over the following centuries to build palaces and churches across Rome, St Peter's among them. The arena floor is missing, which is why you look down into a maze of walls: these are the underground passages where gladiators and caged animals waited, and from which lifts worked by ropes and counterweights raised them through trapdoors into the sand.

Inside the Colosseum: what is left of the seating, tier above tier. Photo: Daryl Mitchell, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

The Roman Forum

A long valley of columns, arches and foundations that was, for centuries, the centre of public life: law courts, temples, the Senate house, the platform where speeches were made. Walk the Via Sacra, the street triumphal processions took, from the Arch of Titus down to the Arch of Septimius Severus. Look closely at the inside of the Arch of Titus, where a carved relief shows soldiers carrying the treasures of the Temple of Jerusalem through Rome. Further on are the round Temple of Vesta and the courtyard of the House of the Vestals, lined with statues of the priestesses who kept the city's sacred fire.

Inside the Arch of Titus: the spoils of Jerusalem carried through Rome. Photo: Anthony M., via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Palatine Hill

The quiet part, and the one most people skip because they are tired. It should not be skipped. This is where the emperors built their palaces, and the word palace itself comes from the name of the hill. Up here there is shade from umbrella pines, far fewer people, and two of the best views in Rome: down over the whole Forum on one side, and over the Circus Maximus, the chariot racing track, on the other.

The Forum from the Palatine: the view most visitors miss. Photo: Chalaph, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In what order

Entry to the Colosseum is for a fixed time, so the day is built around that slot. Two orders work well:

  • Colosseum first, early. Take the first slot you can get, when the arena is cooler and emptier, then cross to the Forum and finish on the Palatine as the morning groups thin out.
  • Palatine and Forum first, Colosseum late. In summer this keeps you under the trees of the Palatine during the hottest hours and puts you in the Colosseum in the softer light of late afternoon.

Either way, allow about an hour for the Colosseum and two to two and a half hours for the Forum and the Palatine together. There is almost no shade in the Forum and very little to buy once you are inside, so bring water (there are drinking fountains to refill it), a hat in summer, and shoes that can handle large, uneven paving stones.

Why a guide matters more here than almost anywhere

The Colosseum explains itself. The Forum does not. Without a story to hang them on, its ruins are a field of broken columns with Latin names, and many visitors walk through in twenty minutes and wonder what they missed. A guide turns the three columns on the corner into the temple where the state treasury was kept, and the bare brick hall into the place where the Senate sat.

That guide does not have to be a person. An audio tour in your phone follows your position, tells the story of each stop as you reach it, and lets you set the pace: sit on a wall on the Palatine for as long as you like, skip what does not interest you. It costs a fraction of a guided group and needs nothing but earphones and a charged battery. A live guide is still the better choice if you want to ask questions, or if you are travelling with children who need someone to hold their attention.

These are the audio walks and tickets our partner sells for the Colosseum and ancient Rome, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="colosseum" match="colosseum,ancient,gladiators" limit="6"]

One thing to check before you book. Most of these are audio walks without an entry ticket: they guide you around and between the monuments, and you buy your entry separately. A few include it, and their description lists exactly what is covered, so read the "included" section before you pay. Some also continue beyond the ancient site into the city, as far as the Pantheon or the Trevi Fountain, which makes a full day of it.

Practical notes

  • Entry to the three sites is sold as one combined ticket, with a set time for the Colosseum. Dates sell out in high season, so book before you travel.
  • Everyone passes a security check at the Colosseum. Large bags and suitcases are not admitted, and there is no cloakroom.
  • The nearest metro stop is Colosseo, on line B, directly opposite the amphitheatre.
  • Opening hours follow the daylight and change through the year. The current ones are on our page for the Colosseum.

From here

Just outside stands the Arch of Constantine, raised in 315 and free to look at from every side. The Capitoline Hill, with some of the oldest public museums in the world, rises at the far end of the Forum, and the Pantheon is a twenty minute walk beyond it. To see what else is close, open everything there is to do in Rome, or look at the attractions map of Italy if Rome is one stop on a longer trip.

The other side of the hill: the Circus Maximus. Photo: Livioandronico2013, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Cover photo: FeaturedPics, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Does a Colosseum ticket include the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill?
faqs.a: Yes. Entry is sold as one combined ticket for the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill, with a set entry time for the Colosseum.

faqs.q: How long does it take to visit the Colosseum, the Roman Forum and the Palatine Hill?
faqs.a: About three to three and a half hours: around one hour for the Colosseum and two to two and a half hours for the Forum and the Palatine together.

faqs.q: Is an audio tour of the Colosseum and the Forum worth it?
faqs.a: For the Roman Forum especially, yes. Its ruins are hard to read without an explanation. An audio tour in your phone tells the story of each stop at your own pace and costs much less than a guided group.

faqs.q: Do Colosseum audio tours include the entry ticket?
faqs.a: Most do not. They are commentary only, and you buy your entry separately. A few include it: the description of each one lists what is covered, so read it before you book.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Colosseum?
faqs.a: The first entry slot of the morning is the coolest and least crowded. In summer, late afternoon also works well, with the Palatine Hill and its shade earlier in the day.
